data.title: Five or More Coffees a Day Raise Bone Health Concerns for Women
data.incipit: [Above image is unrelated to the article. Clipart Korea.] Kim Dong-woo, Director of Ilsan Jaseng Hospital of Korean MedicineOne cup to wake up after arriving at the office, another after lunch, and one more...
data.body: [Above image is unrelated to the article. Clipart Korea.] Kim Dong-woo, Director of Ilsan Jaseng Hospital of Korean Medicine One cup to wake up after arriving at the office, another after lunch, and one more to shake off the afternoon slump. Add meetings and chats with colleagues, and three or four cups a day come easily. As coffee has settled deep into the daily routine of office workers, women past middle age may want to take a look at how much they are drinking. A study has found that older women who drink too much coffee can show lower bone density. A research team at Flinders University in Australia, in a study published in the international journal Nutrients, tracked coffee and tea consumption and changes in bone density among 9,704 women aged 65 and over for about 10 years. Women who drank more than five cups of coffee a day tended to show lower bone density, the study found. In contrast, drinking about two to three cups a day showed no clear link to bone density. The research team said the findings do not mean people should quit coffee, but that excessive intake beyond five cups a day warrants caution. Women in particular need to pay closer attention to bone health as they age. Around menopause, secretion of the female hormone estrogen declines, causing bone density to fall rapidly. When bone density drops and progresses to osteoporosis, even a minor impact is more likely to cause a fracture. The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency's 2024 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey also found osteoporosis in about one in three women aged 65 and over. Lower bone density means weakened bones and a higher chance of fracture. A leading example is a vertebral compression fracture, in which a vertebra is pressed from above and below and collapses flat. It can occur from something as slight as a sneeze or a light fall on the buttocks. The problem is that treating such fractures is not easy for middle-aged women. When pain is severe, surgery to inject medical cement into the bone is considered, but it carries risks of cement leakage and fractures in adjacent vertebrae. Yet lying down for long stretches until the bone knits weakens the back muscles and ligaments, which can bring on other musculoskeletal disorders. For this reason, integrative Korean medicine treatment focused on conservative care rather than surgery can be effective. In a study published in the international journal Medicine, a research team at Jaseng Hospital of Korean Medicine tracked 166 patients with vertebral compression fractures over an extended period and analyzed the course of integrative Korean medicine treatment. The numeric rating scale (NRS) for lower back pain fell 1.85 points, from 5.75 before treatment to 3.90. The Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), which measures the degree of lower back functional impairment, also dropped about 21 points, from 48.92 to the 27.6 range, while the EQ-5D, a measure of quality of life, improved from 0.59 to 0.75. Because coffee is a drink that is easy to enjoy in everyday life, what matters is taking a look at your own habits rather than quitting outright. After middle age in particular, bone density declines gradually even without visible symptoms, so small everyday habits can shape bone health later on. Start by counting how many cups you drink a day, cut back on excessive intake little by little, and check your current bone condition through regular bone density tests. Keeping both a life with coffee and a healthy old age comes down to moderate intake and steady management.

data.title: Immunization clinic to be hosted after hepatitis A case detected at Winnipeg school
data.incipit: Manitoba·NewA case of hepatitis A was recently diagnosed at a Winnipeg school where an immunization clinic will soon be held to help prevent the spread of the virus.Parents, staff at Shaughnessy Park School...
data.body: Manitoba · New A case of hepatitis A was recently diagnosed at a Winnipeg school where an immunization clinic will soon be held to help prevent the spread of the virus. Parents, staff at Shaughnessy Park School asked to monitor symptoms of acute live infection until Nov. 3 CBC News · Posted: Sep 19, 2026 5:16 PM EDT | Last Updated: 24 minutes ago Listen to this article Estimated 2 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. A file photo shows a kindergarten class. The Winnipeg School Division has confirmed a case of hepatitis A was recently diagnosed at Shaughnessy Park school. (Josée Ducharme/Radio-Canada) A case of hepatitis A was recently diagnosed at a Winnipeg school where an immunization clinic will soon be held to help prevent the spread of the virus. Parents, guardians and staff from Shaughnessy Park School are being asked to monitor for symptoms of the acute liver infection until Nov. 3, according to a memo shared by the Winnipeg Regional Health Authority on Friday. The Winnipeg School Division, which oversees Shaughnessy Park, confirmed the case with CBC. Superintendent Matt Henderson said the division is closely following guidance from public health and an immunization clinic is coming to the school which offers classes for students from nursery to grade 8. It is unclear who contracted the infection and their current condition. Manitoba Public Health says hepatitis A can easily spread by drinking water or eating food that has been contaminated by the feces of an infected person. The infection is common in areas where there's poor sanitation, but improper hand washing or food handling can also facilitate the spread. The province has seen a rise in hepatitis A cases. There have been 898 reported infections between September 2024 and mid-July, according to the latest data from public health. Over that time, seven people have died in connection to the virus, eight patients have been admitted to the intensive care unit and 197 have been hospitalized. Some people with hepatitis A, especially children, might not develop symptoms, public health has said. But if they develop, the onset is abrupt and can include fever, loss of appetite, vomiting, dark urine and yellowing of the skin and eyes. People with a severe illness can have symptoms for several months, while those with mild symptoms often recover within one to two weeks, according to public health.

data.title: LA Union Station travelers may have been exposed to measles by infected passenger, health officials warned
data.incipit: HEALTH & FITNESSL.A. County health officials warned Friday that people who were at Union Station during a 4-hour period last weekend may have been exposed to measles.Saturday, September 19, 2026 9:20PMLOS...
data.body: HEALTH & FITNESS L.A. County health officials warned Friday that people who were at Union Station during a 4-hour period last weekend may have been exposed to measles. Saturday, September 19, 2026 9:20PM LOS ANGELES (CNS) -- Los Angeles County health officials warned Friday that people who were at Union Station during a four-hour period last weekend may have been exposed to measles by an infected train passenger. The passenger, whose name was not released, arrived at the station aboard Amtrak's Southwest Chief Train 3 at 7:03 a.m. Saturday and left at 10:55 a.m. aboard Amtrak Thruway Bus Route 5717 bound for Bakersfield, according to the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health. People who were at Union Station between 8 a.m. and noon Saturday may be at risk of developing measles seven to 21 days after exposure, health officials said. People who have previously had measles or received the recommended measles vaccine are likely protected but should still monitor for symptoms. Those who are unimmunized or whose measles immunization status is unknown are at higher risk and should monitor closely for symptoms, according to the department. The last day to monitor for symptoms is Oct. 3. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, California Department of Public Health and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are working with county health departments to inform passengers seated near the infected traveler on the train or bus of their risk of developing measles. "As measles cases increase, it is important that residents take steps to make sure they are fully protected," Los Angeles County Health Officer Dr. Muntu Davis said. "The MMR vaccine is the safest and most reliable way to prevent measles and protect yourself, your family, and your community." Measles spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs or sneezes. Common symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, red and watery eyes and a rash that typically develops three to five days after other symptoms. The Department of Public Health advised people who develop symptoms to stay home and avoid school, work and gatherings and to call a health care provider immediately. People who may have been exposed were advised not to enter a health care facility without calling first. Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine are 97% effective against measles, while one dose is 93% effective, according to the Department of Public Health. As of Friday, 3,471 measles cases and four measles-associated deaths had been reported nationwide this year, along with 39 outbreaks. Nine percent of the cases required hospitalization for treatment of measles complications or isolation. Copyright 2026, City News Service, Inc. Copyright © 2026 by City News Service, Inc. data.title: How runaway AI agents could pose an existential threat to humanity
data.incipit: Safety advocates and researchers have warned of catastrophic consequences if the rapid advancement of frontier artificial intelligence goes unchecked.For instance, AI threatens to multiply harm...
data.body: SINGAPORE – Safety advocates and researchers have warned of catastrophic consequences if the rapid advancement of frontier artificial intelligence goes unchecked. For instance, AI threatens to multiply harm across bioterrorism, cyberwarfare, mass disinformation and advanced weaponry. The Straits Times unpacks these four existential threats and the push for control. Bioterrorism General-purpose models such as OpenAI’s GPT-5 and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 can analyse scientific literature and data, reason through research problems and suggest experiments. This sophisticated capability has heightened fears that the technology could be used to develop biological weapons. More specialised tools such as OpenAI’s GPT-Rosalind can also speed up drug discovery and genomics, while Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold and AlphaGenome can help scientists understand proteins and DNA. Specialised knowledge once confined to trained scientists is now accessible to those with little or no biological expertise. Highlighting how these risks could play out, The New York Times reported in April how chatbots were prompted to provide step-by-step information on obtaining biological materials and turning them into weapons to be set off in public places. The report featured Stanford University biosecurity expert David Relman, who said that a chatbot explained in vivid detail how to modify a pathogen into a dangerous drug-resistant superbug and take advantage of a security lapse in public transport to maximise casualties without getting caught. Safeguards were added later to the chatbot. Indeed, the latest threat intelligence report by Anthropic in September revealed that researchers used its Claude model for questionable experiments. These included attempts to make the chikungunya virus more transmissible and immune-evasive, as well as efforts to adapt highly pathogenic bird flu to mammals. Anthropic said some researchers even tried to evade safeguards or obscure the purpose of their work, highlighting the difficulty of policing the technology that has both good and harmful applications. However, AI chatbots cannot autonomously create a biological weapon. Underscoring this point, US policy research organisation RAND said in a 2025 report that turning AI-generated knowledge into a working biological weapon would still require specialised expertise and the ability to translate instructions into physical laboratory work. Cyberattacks Software vulnerabilities allow attackers to find a way into systems, steal credentials, move deeper into the network, extract data and stay undetected. AI can perform many of these steps faster, and even automatically. In July, Check Point Research said it recorded instances over the past 12 months where AI autonomously executed attacks, including one on nine Mexican government agencies. The attacker used Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 to probe systems, exploit vulnerabilities, map networks and escalate their access once inside. Some 400 million tax, civil registry, vehicle, patient and electoral records between December 2025 and February 2026 were compromised. The attacker simply gave the AI chatbots tasks and left them to work out the steps in between. Anthropic’s report also detailed a Chinese-speaking hacker group that targeted about 50 organisations worldwide, including government agencies and organisations running critical infrastructure. The hackers used swarms of autonomous AI agents to conduct parallel operations. A lead agent divided a hacking job into smaller tasks – such as scouting targets and compromised networks – and assigned them to sub-agents. This set-up allowed the agents to discover more than a dozen unknown vulnerabilities in network equipment in a month. Anthropic subsequently banned all accounts linked to the hackers and introduced additional monitoring to detect similar automated activity. But AI agents can also be trained to hunt down rogue ones. In August, OpenAI launched GPT-5.6-Cyber for approved cybersecurity professionals to find vulnerabilities and fix them before attackers can exploit them. OpenAI said the model uncovered unknown vulnerabilities in the engine powering Google Chrome, which Google fixed. Weapons and warfare In November 2025, Reuters reported that both Ukrainian and Russian forces had deployed AI-assisted drones that use onboard cameras and computer vision to lock onto targets. The fear is that such AI-powered autonomous weapons could independently decide who to kill. In its threat intelligence report, Anthropic said Russia-based developers had used Claude to build software for an autonomous swarm of kamikaze drones that could coordinate with one another. The developers had also loaded the software onto real hardware for simulations. Anthropic subsequently banned the accounts linked to the project. Some countries have already set limits on AI involvement on the battlefield. Both the US and Britain require appropriate human oversight over such autonomous weapons, which can identify, select and attack targets. Moves are also under way to establish legally binding international rules for autonomous weapons. In August, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and International Committee of the Red Cross president Mirjana Spoljaric called on countries to begin negotiations on such an agreement. Influence campaigns AI has been used in influence campaigns since 2024, when OpenAI first uncovered operations linked to Russia, China, Iran and Israel using its models to generate articles and social media posts. Similarly, Microsoft found China-linked actors using AI-generated images, audio and video to target voters. More capable AI models now allow faster automation at scale. Anthropic disclosed in its report that it had disrupted an operation linked to the France-based digital advertising agency LKM Company. The agency used Claude to produce and rewrite political content across about 70 fake news websites for paying clients. The network published at least 8,913 articles in about 20 languages, supported by social media accounts and more than 250 fake accounts posing as commenters. But Anthropic said the operation secured little engagement from real users before it was dismantled. In the same report, Anthropic said it uncovered an Iran-focused influence operation that fed Claude about 8,400 Telegram posts by a real activist to imitate his writing style. The AI-assisted account then impersonated the activist in live political conversations with his contacts, who appeared unaware of foul play. But efforts have stepped up to counter such campaigns. AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI monitor their services for influence operations, ban malicious accounts and share threat intelligence with law enforcement and their peers. Governments and social media platforms have started to make AI-generated material easier to identify. Under the European Union AI Act rules that went live in August, AI-generated text, images and video reaching European users must carry clear disclosures identifying them as artificial. At the same time, social media platforms are rolling out their own verification tools. For instance, YouTube automatically labels videos it detects as synthetic, while X lets users flag misleading posts and add context to curb misinformation.

data.body: The official DRC Ministry of Communication and Media account posted a September 17, 2026 Ebola situation report detailing the outbreak across 7 provinces (Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, Sud-Ubangi) and 62 health zones. Key stats show 7,541 confirmed cases, 1,823 recoveries, 3,639 deaths (48.3% fatality rate), 930 patients hospitalized or isolated, and 87.2% contact tracing success. Positive updates include 25 new recoveries in the last 24 hours, no new geographic foci identified, and vaccination progress with 3,063 doses in Tshopo and 708 in Bas-Uélé; the public is urged to call 151 for suspected symptoms.

data.title: Preventing, protecting yourself from flu this season
data.incipit: This flu season started earlier than usual this year, and doctors say now is the time to make sure you are protecting yourself.According to doctors, the best way to do that is by getting the flu shot before...
data.body: This flu season started earlier than usual this year, and doctors say now is the time to make sure you are protecting yourself. According to doctors, the best way to do that is by getting the flu shot before cases really start picking up. Allergist Christina Barnes says October is a good time to get your flu shot. She says protection lasts for about six months, helping cover much of the upcoming flu season. Even when the vaccine isn't a perfect match for the strains circulating, she says it can still lower the risk of getting sick and needing medical care or hospitalization. This flu season started earlier than usual this year, and doctors say now is the time to make sure you are protecting yourself. (WSBT video) "So even though last year is a good example, for instance, last year wasn't a great match, but it still reduced the chance of getting the flu. It still reduced the chance of having to go to the doctor for the flu, so being sick enough to go to the doctor, and it reduced the chance of having to be in the hospital. So even when there's not a great match, it still is worth it," said Christina Barnes, MD, allergist and immunologist. According to Barnes, body aches and a fever are signs you're likely dealing with something other than allergies. She also recommends washing your hands, avoiding people who are sick when possible and staying home if you're experiencing those symptoms to avoid spreading illness. The flu shot is generally recommended by doctors for people six months and older, with some exceptions.

data.title: Miguel Bronchud: New Data on Germline EGFR T790M and Non-Smoker Lung Cancer Risk
data.incipit: Miguel Bronchud, Veteran Cancer Clinician and Researcher, shared on LinkedIn: “Lung cancer in non smokers might rarely be the consequence of germ line mutations in the EGFR gene? USA 23andMe database, a...
data.body: Miguel Bronchud , Veteran Cancer Clinician and Researcher, shared on LinkedIn : “ Lung cancer in non smokers might rarely be the consequence of germ line mutations in the EGFR gene ? USA 23andMe database, a population-scale biobank containing genomic data for 3.3 million participants, allowed to study the distribution, effects, and history of the haplotype containing T790. On page 1208 in the recent SCIENCE issue, LoPiccolo et al. (Science 393, 1208 (2026)) report a population-scale analysis of a rare germline variant that is associated with high risk of lung cancer (without smoking cigarettes or cigars). In addition to confirming its effects on lung cancer risk, the study uses historical and demographic data to uncover its history. Two decades ago, a group of rare germline variants in the same stretch of DNA (haplotype) in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene were identified as risk factors for lung cancer EGFR is a well-established oncogene with several common cancer-associated somatic (nongermline) variants that can be targeted with anticancer drugs . It encodes a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes normal cell growth, but a single mutation on one chromosome in a somatic cell can lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation and cancer. Nearly all somatic mutations in EGFR that have been documented in lung cancer tissue are lethal at the embryonic stage if they occur in germ cells. However, one of these variants, T790M, is not lethal during embryonic development. And, to make this rare germ line mutation even more interesting , this variant occurs in families with incomplete penetrance, which means that some individuals who inherited T790M can reach old age without developing lung cancer. In fact , T790M in somatic cells can contribute to resistance to targeted anticancer therapy . As elegantly explained in an editorial in the same SCIENCE, LoPiccolo et al. (2026) very cleverly used the 23andMe database, a population-scale biobank containing genomic data for 3.3 million participants, to study the distribution, effects, and history of the haplotype containing T790M, which has been well characterized. This type of study avoids some of the biases of studies that enroll participants on the basis of disease status, such as family studies or small case-control studies. The scale of the database allows a different approach from the method typically used to characterize founder effects Instead – HERE the Novelty – the authors gathered data from hundreds of individuals carrying a single copy of T790M (heterozygotes) . RESULTS: For most carriers of T790M, the variant resided on a long, shared segment of DNA that had the hallmarks of European ancestry. The authors also found that the neighboring genetic variants on this haplotype do not contribute to the effect of T790M.” You can also read: STAS in Stage I Lung Adenocarcinoma Is More Than a Histologic Finding: Multi-Omic Profiling Reveals an Aggressive Molecular Phenotype

data.title: Fiji HIV crisis: The dangerous ‘bluetoothing’ trend driving the epidemic
data.incipit: A dangerous drug-sharing trend is driving Fiji’s HIV epidemic, a top Pacific health expert says. Fiji’s Government this week declared an HIV national emergency after figures showed that one in 60 people now...
data.body: A dangerous drug-sharing trend is driving Fiji’s HIV epidemic, a top Pacific health expert says. Fiji’s Government this week declared an HIV national emergency after figures showed that one in 60 people now have the virus. Among pregnant women, the figure is one in 50. It is one of the world’s fastest-growing HIV epidemics. Pasifika doctor, Sir Collin Tukuitonga, said he had never heard of the drug-sharing trend - known as bluetoothing - until a doctor from Fiji explained it at a medical conference where the surge in HIV cases in Fiji was being discussed. Sharing blood for the same high “They were talking about this thing called bluetoothing, where someone will take whatever - a drug - and then they take the blood from themselves and inject it into their friend. “It’s a way of sharing the drug because they can’t really afford the supply. So they share the drug.” The name for the drug-sharing 'bluetooth' trend comes from bluetooth wireless technology, where data is shared between devices. Photo / File Bluetoothing - also known as hotspotting - is a term taken from bluetooth wireless technology, where information is shared between cell phones. Drug-users have adapted it into slang to describe the transfer of drug-infused blood from one body to another using a shared needle for a cheaper high. Tukuitonga, the director of Te Poutoko Ora a Kiwi Centre for Pacific and Global Health, said a second doctor from Papua New Guinea, who spoke at the same doctors’ conference, also referred to bluetoothing. Tukuitonga said it was a “very sad” development in Fiji’s HIV crisis. He said some young people were not aware of the dangers of needle-sharing. “It’s not being spread in the way HIV traditionally is spread - sexual transmission and mother to child. “The latest outbreak in Fiji is actually the result of drug use; it’s occurred mainly in young Fijian men who inject drugs. A lot of it relates to poverty, lack of education and lack of jobs.” Top Pasifika health doctor and expert, Sir Collin Tukuitonga. Photo / University of Auckland Tukuitonga said the cultural stigma and taboo around HIV and AIDS being associated with being gay also meant many people would avoid getting tested because of that perceived connection. “But the most recent outbreak in Fiji is not so much a gay man’s problem. It’s a drug user’s problem.” Fijian Health Minister, Dr Antonio Lalabalavu this week said the introduction of extra testing stations around the country was helping to identify more cases. Known drug users will also have access to clean needles to help stop bloodborne transmission - something that has been controversial in the island nation. Officials, however, say it is about helping people and are calling on the public to put an end to social shaming. “This is about protecting people - not judging them, not watching them, not shaming them,” Lalabalavu said. Vaimoana Mase is the Pasifika editor for the Herald’s Talanoa section , sharing stories from the Pacific community. She won junior reporter of the year at the then Qantas Media Awards in 2010 and won the best opinion writing award at the 2023 Voyager Media Awards.

data.title: Parts of Kalamazoo under boil advsory after e. coli bacteria found in sample
data.incipit: A boil water advisory has been issued for parts of Kalamazoo after E. coli bacteria was found in a water sample.The city is doing more sampling to determine the extent of the problem and trying to find the...
data.body: A boil water advisory has been issued for parts of Kalamazoo after E. coli bacteria was found in a water sample. The city is doing more sampling to determine the extent of the problem and trying to find the source of the contamination, according to a release on the city's website . The advisory applies only to people consuming water within the city of Kalamazoo's low and high pressure districts as shown below. The boil water advisory applies only to people consuming water within the city of Kalamazoo's Low and High pressure districts, as shown in this map. Water customers in the affected area should bring tap water to a rolling boil and boil it for at least two minutes before using it for drinking, making ice, preparing food, brushing teeth, washing dishes, or other consumptive purposes, the release says. The presence of E. coli indicates that the water may be contaminated with human or animal wastes, which can cause short-term effects, such as diarrhea, cramps, nausea, headaches, or other symptoms. The contaminants may pose a greater health risk for infants, young children, some of the elderly, and people with severely-compromised immune systems, the release says The advisory will remain in effect until the city determines that the water is safe for normal use. This article originally appeared on The Detroit News: Parts of Kalamazoo under boil advsory after e. coli bacteria found in sample
